title: Min, Max and Sum as a Value Tuple
statement:
A function that needs to hand back three related numbers at once has,
traditionally, three bad options: pack them into an array and hope the
caller remembers which index is which, define a one-off class just to carry
three fields home, or take three `out` parameters and clutter the call
site. C#'s **value tuples** are the fourth option, built for exactly this:
a lightweight, named, temporary bundle that exists for the length of one
return trip.

## Your function

```
public static (int Min, int Max, long Sum) Stats(int[] values);
```

`values` has at least one element. Return a tuple of its minimum, its
maximum, and the sum of all its elements.

## Watch out

- **The sum is a `long`, the elements are `int`.** `values` can hold up to
  a few million elements, each up to `int.MaxValue` -- summed as `int` that
  overflows and wraps to a nonsense negative number long before the array
  is exhausted. Accumulate into the `long` the return type already commits
  you to, not into an `int` you then convert at the end.
- **`Min` and `Max` come from the values actually in the array**, not from
  `int.MinValue`/`int.MaxValue` as starting points left unchecked -- an
  array that happens to be entirely negative, or entirely positive, is a
  fixed test precisely because a wrong choice of starting point can survive
  unnoticed on an array that straddles zero.
- The tuple's element names (`Min`, `Max`, `Sum`) are part of the
  signature -- construct it as `(min, max, sum)` positionally, or
  `(Min: min, Max: max, Sum: sum)` explicitly; either produces the same
  tuple, since the names are compile-time metadata, not data the values
  carry with them.

tests.name: an all-negative array -- min/max cannot both come from int.MaxValue
an all-positive array -- the mirror case
a sum that overflows a 32-bit int but not a 64-bit long
tests.description: 6,000,000,000 is past int.MaxValue (~2.1 billion) -- accumulating as int wraps to a negative number.
